activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard modern piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
Grandma's piano sat in the front room under a lace cloth, and Avery had been told she could practice on it all summer. The only problem was that her lesson book had gone missing somewhere between her house and here, and Mr. Perera, the neighbour who tuned pianos, was coming over in an hour to fix a sticky key.

"Can't you just play without the book?" asked Yusra, who had come along to keep her company.

Avery ran her fingers over the keys. "I only know three songs, and they're all in the book." She frowned at the keyboard, thinking. On FaceTime last week, Ty had bragged that his cousin knew every piano in the world had the same number of keys. Ty liked to exaggerate, so Avery had half believed him and half not. Here was a way to find out. "Help me count these," she said. "You do the white ones, I'll do the black ones."

They started from the left end. Yusra tapped each white key with one finger, whispering numbers, while Avery hopped her finger from black key to black key, up over the hills and down into the valleys. The room was quiet except for their counting and the sparse ticking of the old clock on the shelf. When they finished, Yusra said, "Fifty-two." Avery checked her own total twice, because it seemed small. "Thirty-six." She added them together on the scratch paper. "Eighty-eight."

"That's what Ty said," Yusra reported, holding up her phone. She had texted him mid-count, and he had replied almost instantly, as if he'd been waiting. "He says a standard modern piano has 88 keys, 52 white and 36 black. He copied it from his cousin."

"So he was right," Avery said, and something about that made her feel the piano differently, like it wasn't one long mystery but a pattern she could learn. If every piano in the world had the same 88 keys, then a song she learned here would work on any piano anywhere.

The doorbell rang, and Mr. Perera came in carrying his tool bag. "Sticky key, is it?" he asked, and Avery suddenly perceived the problem she could actually solve today. She pointed at the E she'd been avoiding all morning. "This one. I can show you exactly which it is, because I counted."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A cast saw's blade vibrates rapidly back and forth instead of spinning, which lets it cut hard plaster or fiberglass without cutting the skin underneath.
story:
Asher drummed the fingers of his right hand on his desk, which was the only hand he could drum with, since the left one had been in a fiberglass cast for six weeks. Ms. Okonkwo had written CAST OFF TODAY on the board beside the date, because half the class had made him promise to describe it. The appointment was at two thirty, and his mother would leave without him if he was not at the office by two fifteen, since she had a meeting she refused to miss.

"Are you scared?" Wilson asked from the next row. "My cousin said they cut it off with a saw. A real saw, the loud kind."

"That sounds toxic," Nikki said, shaking her head. "Like, actual dangerous."

Asher looked down at his cast. He had signed it in green marker and drawn a shark on it, and underneath the fiberglass his arm was fine. He thought about the saw his dentist used, the one that spun and screamed and was only safe because it stopped the instant it touched anything soft. A cast saw would touch skin the whole way down. Unless it was not that kind of saw at all. He could not see inside the machine, but he could test the idea when he got there.

"I have an idea about it," he said. "I'll illustrate. Ask me tomorrow." Ms. Okonkwo raised an eyebrow at the murmur around him and pointed at the clock. He packed his binder one-handed and hurried out.

At the clinic the nurse wheeled over a tray with the saw on it, and a small kid two chairs away began to cry the moment it buzzed. "It won't cut you," the nurse told him. "The blade vibrates back and forth instead of spinning. It cuts the hard cast, but not skin underneath."

Asher held out his arm. "Can you show me on my hand first?" he asked. She pressed the humming blade flat against his palm and dragged it along his skin. It was warm and ticklish, like a phone buzzing, and it left no mark at all. He grinned at the small kid, who had gone quiet. Then the nurse slid the blade into the cast, and a long crack ran down the fiberglass over the shark drawing.

"Want to keep the pieces?" she asked, already reaching for the shears.

activity: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
knowledge_domain: to follow a recipe to bake muffins from start to finish including preheating the oven
fact: The muffin method mixes the dry ingredients in one bowl and the wet ingredients in another, then combines them only at the end.
story:
The restaurant kitchen smelled like onions and dish soap, which Levi decided was not the correct smell for muffins but was going to have to do. Ms. Eze had left a recipe card on the steel counter, a bag of flour, eggs, a carton of buttermilk, and a note that said only "Oven. 400. You first." Raven leaned against the walk-in fridge eating a pickle she had found somewhere, and Izabella was already reading the card like it was a test she intended to pass.

Levi cracked both eggs into the big bowl, poured in the buttermilk, dumped the flour on top, and started stirring with the confidence of a person who had never once thought about batter. The spoon turned on him almost immediately. Something pasty clung to it in ridges. Something wet sloshed underneath, indifferent to his efforts, refusing to become anything at all. He stirred harder. It got worse.

"Step two says whisk the dry ingredients in one bowl," Izabella read, in the voice of someone delivering bad news gently. "Step three says the wet ones in a different bowl. It says combine at the end." She looked into his bowl, then at him, then back at the card, as if one of the three might explain the other two. Raven peered in over his shoulder. "It's making little flour islands," she said. "That one has a moat."

Levi stared at the lumps and tried to isolate the problem, the way Ms. Eze was always telling him to do instead of panicking. Two bowls, mixed separately, joined only at the end. That was the whole idea, apparently, and he had skipped it. He couldn't see inside a lump to know what had gone wrong in there, but he could test it. He scraped the miserable batter into the trash, measured flour, baking powder, sugar and salt into the big bowl, cracked eggs and poured buttermilk and oil into a smaller one, and kept them apart like two kids who could not sit together yet. Then, at the very end, he poured wet into dry and folded. The batter came together smooth and thick, with no moats anywhere.

The muffins rose into golden domes while Raven stood at the oven window guarding them as if they might escape. When Ms. Eze came back and bit into one, she chewed slowly, and Levi held his breath, trying to read her face for a motive he could not see. She took a second muffin without a word. Raven nudged him. "That," she whispered, "is the review."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Chicago's Engine Company 21 is widely credited with the first fire pole, installed in 1878 after a firefighter slid down a pole faster than others could take the stairs.
story:
Louis had been waiting for the museum trip for weeks, mostly because of one exhibit: a real fire pole, brass and shiny, rising up through a hole in the ceiling beside a rebuilt fire station from long ago. On the bus, Christina argued with Leen about which was faster, sliding down a pole or running down stairs, and it got loud enough that Ms. Nowak had to intervene and move Leen to a different seat. Louis didn't say anything. He just kept wondering. Why would anyone put a pole through a floor in the first place? Stairs worked fine everywhere else, didn't they?

The class swept through the rooms in a clump. In the nature hall, Leen stopped at a slice of rotting log and read aloud that decomposers like fungi and beetles break down dead wood into fertile soil, which made Louis think about how much of the world happens where you can't see it, underground, inside things. He filed that thought away. On the way out, a guide was standing at the fire station exhibit, tapping the brass pole with one finger.

"Guess why stations once had poles instead of stairs," she said. "Anyone?"

"Because poles look cool?" said Leen.

"Because stairs were too expensive?" said Christina.

Louis stepped closer. He noticed the pole went straight down from the sleeping floor above, no turns, no steps, nothing in the way. If speed was the whole point, then straight down had to beat a zigzag. But how would anybody ever prove a thing like that? Someone must have raced a pole against the stairs. He said, "I think somebody slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs, and after that, everybody wanted one."

The guide grinned. "Close. Want to check the plaque?"

Louis leaned in and read it, and his stomach did a small flip. "Chicago's Engine Company 21," he read slowly. "1878. A firefighter slid down a pole faster than the others could take the stairs, and that's credited as the first fire pole."

"Told you poles were faster," said Christina.

"You said cool, not fast," said Leen.

"Both," said Christina, and she put one hand on the brass, right in the middle, where it was worn the shiniest.

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, three spaced periods, called an ellipsis, show where words have been left out of the middle of a quotation.
story:
Riley had read the last page of "Wolf Hollow" twenty minutes ago, but his essay was still blank, and the essay was due tomorrow morning.

"That quote you keep muttering," said Giuliano from the kitchen table, where he was building a bridge out of popsicle sticks for his own project. "You've said it four times. It's long."

"It's the only one that shows the theme," Riley said. "Betty hiding in the woods proves the book is about how people decide who to trust." He found the page again and read aloud: "'She was there, then she wasn't, like something the hill had swallowed, and we stood in the spot where she'd been, not speaking, not moving, until the cold made us turn back.'"

Giuliano laid down a popsicle stick. "That's huge. Ms. Ito said one or two lines, maximum. She gets aggressive about it. Remember when Milo turned in a whole page of quotation?"

"Nothing bad happened to Milo," Riley said.

"He got a negotiation. She said he could revise it or take the zero, and he revised it for two days." Giuliano pushed his bridge aside. "Just cut the middle."

Riley stared at the sentence. The beginning showed the swallowing and the end showed them not moving, both proof that the town couldn't distinguish a real threat from a rumor. The middle, "like something the hill had swallowed," was the pretty part but not the proof. He copied the quotation onto his draft and drew a line through it. The problem was that if he just glued the pieces together, it would look like the book said something it didn't. He flipped through his notes until he found the handout on quotations, and there it was, one line he'd skimmed past in September.

He typed three periods, each one with a space between it and the next, where the cut words had been. "It's called an ellipsis," he said, reading the handout's label aloud.

"Sounds like a dinosaur," Giuliano said, without looking up from his glue.

Riley read the shortened quotation back to himself. "'She was there, then she wasn't . . . and we stood in the spot where she'd been, not speaking, not moving, until the cold made us turn back.'" The theme still stood, and now the quotation fit inside his paragraph with room to spare. He typed his sentence about trust underneath it, saved the file twice, and leaned over to press PRINT.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing guitar strings repeatedly makes the fingertips sore at first; with regular practice, the skin toughens into calluses and playing hurts less.
story:
Kate set her guitar on her lap in Mr. Yip's studio and looked at her fingertips. Eight days of playing had left red dents in the skin, and pressing the strings felt like pressing wire into a sunburn. "I think I'm done," she said. "Maybe piano. Piano keys don't fight back."

Mr. Yip only nodded and wrote something in his book. "Same time next week," he said.

In the waiting room, Kate found Jersey, who had been taking lessons for two years and was tuning his guitar on the bench by the window. She held out her hand, palm up, fingers spread. "Does this happen to everyone, or am I just broken?"

Jersey took her hand and pressed his thumb against the tip of her first finger. She winced. Then he held out his own fingertips, and Kate leaned close. The skin there was thicker, slightly shiny, ridged in little circles. "Mine looked exactly like yours at the start," he said. "Pressing the strings hurts like that at first. If you keep playing, the skin toughens into calluses, and after a while it stops hurting. I barely feel it now."

Kate turned that over in her mind. The soreness had a hidden cause, and the cure was hidden too, something that happened slowly inside the skin where she couldn't watch it. She wanted to verify it before she wasted another week. "So it's not about being tough today," she said. "It's about showing up until the skin changes on its own."

"That's it," Jersey said. "Ask Daniyal. He quit for a month last spring and had to start all over with the sore fingers."

On the drive home, Kate told her mother the whole thing, and then sat in the kitchen drawing a calendar in her notebook. The boxes looked symmetrical, four tidy rows, and in the corner she wrote a crown over the word monarchy because her social studies homework was due Friday and she didn't want to forget it. But most of her mind was on the guitar. She played for fifteen minutes that night, wincing, and marked an X in the first box.

At the next lesson, she played the three chords Mr. Yip had assigned, slowly and evenly, and he raised one eyebrow, which for him was a standing ovation. In the waiting room afterward, she pressed her fingertips against her thumb, checking, and found a small hard spot just beginning on her first finger. She ran to the bench by the window and held her hand out to Jersey. "Feel that," she said. "That's week two of a callus."

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
knowledge_domain: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
fact: In a series circuit, if one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and every bulb in it goes out.
story:
Willow had come to the skate park to ride, but the maker van was parked by the fence again, its folding table covered in batteries, bulbs, and coiled wire, and Ms. Campbell-Brown was waving her over. Today's challenge: build a circuit with a battery, a switch, and a bulb, then explain why the bulb lights. "Once you've got one bulb going," Ms. Campbell-Brown said, "try two."

Willow clipped wires to the battery, added a switch made from a brass fastener, and screwed in the bulb. Nothing. She wiggled the switch, and the bulb flared bright, then dimmed when she let go. So the switch opened and closed something, she thought. Something she couldn't see. What was actually travelling through that wire? She built a second loop with two bulbs in a line, and both glowed, fainter but steady. Evie skidded up on her board, flipped it, and leaned over the table. "Why's yours dimmer than mine was?"

Then Willow's first bulb went dark with a pop, and the second one died at the same instant. "Hey, they both quit," she said. "But only one popped." She stared at the dead pair, chin in her hand. Maybe the electricity had to go around in a loop, through every piece, and back. She unclipped the burnt bulb and bridged the gap with a plain wire. The second bulb lit at once, bright and robust, brighter than before. Javier, who had been watching from the ramp, rolled closer. "So one dead bulb can knock out the whole line?"

"It looks like it," Willow said. "In this kind of circuit, if one bulb breaks, the loop is broken and every bulb in it goes out." She turned to Evie. "So in a string of holiday lights, one bad bulb could black out the whole string. That's a good candidate for why those old strings always went dark." Ms. Campbell-Brown raised an eyebrow but said nothing, only slid a fresh bulb across the table.

Willow screwed it into the empty socket and snapped the switch closed. The string blazed, two warm points of light against the grey afternoon. "Okay," she said, pulling out her notebook. "Now what happens with three?"

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Sleep talking is common in children and usually harmless, and sleep talkers normally have no memory of it the next morning.
story:
Easton stood at the bottom of the stairs holding his sleeping bag like a shield. It was his first sleepover at Mikaela's house, and the basement rec room already looked nothing like a basement. Strings of fairy lights hung from the ceiling, a bowl of popcorn sat on the ping-pong table, and Elena was sprawled on an air mattress with a bag of gummy worms.

"Claim the couch," Mikaela said, tossing him a pillow. "It's the best spot, and you're the guest."

Easton dropped his bag by the couch. Elena narrowed her eyes at him across the room. "Warning. Mikaela talks in her sleep. Last time she gave a whole speech about a hamster election."

"I do not," Mikaela said. "You're making it up to scare the new kid."

Easton said nothing, but he filed it away. He had read something once about sleep talking, and one detail stuck with him: the talker usually remembers nothing by morning. That meant nobody could settle the argument tonight. The proof would have to wait until morning, and somebody would have to be awake enough to catch it. He decided that somebody would be him.

They played ping-pong until their arms ached, Elena proving surprisingly agile, lunging for shots nobody thought she could reach. Then they watched a movie, and one by one they dropped off. Easton fought to stay awake. Around midnight, sure enough, Mikaela's voice floated out of her sleeping bag, muffled and slow: "Ballot box... under the couch... Mr. Nibbles demands a recount." Easton grabbed his phone and recorded ten seconds of it, grinning in the dark. Then, because the floor was cold and Mikaela had kicked her blanket halfway off, he tucked it back over her shoulders before lying down.

At breakfast, Elena pounced. "Hamster election. Recount. We all heard it."

"Impossible," Mikaela said, cheeks going pink. "I would remember saying something that weird. I remember everything I say." She looked at Easton for backup.

Easton pushed his plate of toast aside. "That's the thing. I read that sleep talking is really common in kids, and it's harmless, but the person almost never remembers it the next morning. You wouldn't remember. That doesn't mean it didn't happen." He held out his phone. "But if you don't trust Elena, you can deduce the truth yourself. Listen."

Mikaela pressed play. Her own sleepy voice filled the kitchen, mumbling about Mr. Nibbles and the recount. Her mouth fell open. Then she started to laugh, a real laugh that bent her over the counter, and when she straightened up she pointed at Easton. "Fine. I believe you. But tonight you're sleeping in the rec room, and I'm recording you."

"Deal," Easton said, and stole the last gummy worm from Elena's bag.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Havdalah ceremony uses a cup of wine or grape juice, fragrant spices to smell, and a braided candle with several wicks.
story:
Lydia had noticed something strange about Saturdays. Every week, right before sundown, her mother packed the little box with the juice cup, the spice tin, and the braided candle with several wicks, and instead of staying home, the whole family drove to the cemetery. "Havdalah is for leaving Grandma's Shabbat the way she liked it," Mom always said, and that was all she would say. Lydia's intuition told her there was more to it, some reason hiding underneath, and she decided to test an idea.

That afternoon she carried the box herself up the hill between the rows of stones. Her little brother, who was five, marched behind her with his chin out, because tonight he was allowed to hold the braided candle for the first time. "I won't drop it," he kept saying. "I never drop anything." Lydia privately remembered the dropped bowl of oranges from Tuesday, but she said, "I know. You'll be careful."

They stopped at Grandma's stone. Mom poured grape juice into the cup and set it on the flat top of the granite, and Lydia noticed that Mom always poured before Grandma's name, never after, as if Grandma were being handed the cup first, like a guest. While the shadows stretched long, Lydia asked, "Do the spices signify something? Is that why you pass them around three times?" Mom smiled. "Smell them and wonder," she said. So Lydia smelled the cloves, and her brother sniffed so hard he sneezed, and the sky went from orange to gray to dark blue, and it was time.

Mom lit the candle, all its wicks flickering at once, and placed it in her brother's careful hands. Lydia watched the flames dance over the grave, and she thought she understood: Grandma could not smell the spices or taste the juice, but Mom needed her to be there anyway, every single week, resilient as the stone itself. "Say the blessing," Mom whispered. Lydia's brother lifted the candle higher and said, "For Grandma," and the little flames waved in the wind.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Fresh sweat has almost no smell; body odor comes when bacteria on the skin break down sweat from armpit glands that become active at puberty.
story:
On the drive home from the gym, Hailey sat in the back of Ms. Eze's car between Davin and Darius, her hair still damp, and lifted her wrist to her nose. The sweat there smelled like almost nothing. Then she sniffed the shoulder of her shirt. Not almost nothing. Definitely something.

"You smell like the boys' locker room," Davin said, fanning the window open with his hand.

"You smell the same," Hailey said. "Why do my wrists smell like water but my shirt doesn't? It's all sweat." She turned it over in her head. If sweat itself had the smell, every sweaty part of her should smell the same. Unless the smell wasn't coming from the sweat at all. She remembered Davin complaining last week that he'd never needed deodorant until this year, and what his older cousin had told him. "Your cousin said fresh sweat has almost no smell, right?"

"Yeah. He said body odor comes when bacteria on your skin break down sweat from the glands in your armpits, and those glands don't even turn on until puberty." Davin shrugged. "He was pretty gross about it."

So the smell needed both things: the sweat from those new glands and the bacteria eating it. That gave Hailey an idea she could test. She dug the little bottle of hand sanitizer out of the side pocket of her gym bag and, pretending to fix her sleeve, wiped down her left armpit thoroughly. The right one she left alone. If bacteria were the hidden cause, killing them on one side should change what happened there. Ms. Eze pulled up to a red light and asked what they wanted for dinner, and Darius said, "Thai cuisine, please," with total confidence, so the car argued about noodles until they reached Hailey's street.

In her driveway she ducked down, sniffed each side of her shirt like a scientist checking two samples. Left side: sanitizer and nothing else. Right side: the locker room. That refuted the idea that sweat alone made the stink. The bacteria had to be the difference, and she'd gotten rid of only half of them.

"Hailey, are you sniffing yourself?" Davin leaned over, grinning. "Because I already did that exact experiment last month."

"You did not."

"Check my gym bag," Darius said. "Why do you think it smells like a hospital?"

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Thailand, the head is considered sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a child, can be seen as rude.
story:
Alice stood at the gate of the temple with a wrapped box under her arm, trying to remember everything her mother had told her that morning. Take off your shoes before the main hall. Hold things with your right hand. Don't point your feet at anyone. The box held oranges, because her mother said you never arrive at a festival empty-handed, and Mr. Li, who organized the community lunch, had written a note saying gifts of fruit were always welcome.

Muhammad was waiting by the shoe rack, grinning. "You brought a whole bag of shoes in your head," he said, watching her count her rules out loud. "Nobody will quiz you." He pressed his palms together and bowed slightly toward an elderly woman passing by, and Alice copied him, palms at her chest, and the woman smiled and wai-ed back, her hands higher than Muhammad's. Alice filed that away. Higher hands, she guessed, for someone older.

Inside, the hall smelled of incense and lemongrass. Priya waved them over to a low table where families were sharing rice, curries, and little folded banana-leaf packets. "Sit like this," Priya whispered, tucking her legs sideways so her feet pointed away from the table. "My grandma says feet are the lowest part of you, so you keep them pointing low, at the floor." Alice folded herself sideways too, feeling like a pretzel, and Muhammad passed her a spoon for the curry and a fork for pushing food onto it, which was apparently the proper order, fork in the left hand, spoon in the right.

After lunch, a little boy in a dinosaur shirt came tearing around the pillar, and Alice reached out on instinct to steady him, her hand hovering over his hair. Muhammad caught her wrist, gently but fast. "Don't touch his head. In Thailand the head is sacred, so touching someone's head, even to pat a kid, can be seen as rude." The boy's mother had seen the whole thing, and Alice bowed her head and said, "Khop khun kha," which she had learned meant thank you, and the woman laughed and waved her hands like it was nothing.

Alice kept turning the rule over while she helped stack bowls. She noticed that when the little boy stumbled, the mother crouched and lifted him by the shoulders instead of scooping him up by the head, the way Alice's own dad did. Same rule, everywhere here. When Mr. Li passed by, Alice tested it, offering a mandarin with her right hand and a small bow, and he received it with two hands and a nod. One for one, like a code.

That evening she wrote a card to Muhammad's grandmother, who had cooked the curry. "Dear Khun Yai, thank you for the best lunch of my whole year. I used my spoon right and I did not touch anybody's head. Alice." She drew a wai-ing stick figure at the bottom and asked Muhammad to deliver it. "I'll add one thing," he said, borrowing her pen, and wrote underneath, "She's officially family now." Alice tucked the card into her backpack pocket, right next to her spare shoes.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: A greenstick fracture is a break where the bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch; it happens mostly in children because their bones are more flexible.
story:
Hailey sat in the back seat of the family car with her new orange cast propped on a pillow, waiting for Olivia's mom to pull away from the curb. Olivia climbed in beside her, careful with her backpack, and stared at the cast the whole ride.

"Ms. Tan told everyone you broke your arm," Olivia said. "But my brother said you told him it was only partly broken. That's weird. How can a bone be partly broken?"

Hailey had wondered the same thing in the emergency room, until the doctor said the words. "It's called a greenstick fracture," she told her. "The bone cracks on one side and bends on the other, like a young green branch. It mostly happens to kids because our bones are more flexible."

Olivia frowned. "So one side is cracked and the other side just... bends?"

"Exactly. That's why it looks crooked on the x-ray instead of snapped clean through." Hailey wiggled her fingers out of the top of the cast. "At first I thought the doctor was being nice to me. Like, telling me it was only partly broken so I wouldn't panic."

"That's so naive," Olivia said, then looked sorry. "I mean, not you. Just thinking a doctor would do that."

"Whatever," Hailey said, grinning. "The real plague of the whole thing is not being able to write. I have a quiz in math on Friday and I can't even hold a pencil."

Olivia was quiet for a moment, watching the trees go by the window. Then she dug through her backpack and pulled out a fat marker and a thin notebook. "You can still hold this," she said, pressing the marker into Hailey's good hand. "I'll write down everything Ms. Tan says tomorrow, and after school I'll read you my notes and you can answer out loud. Practice that way."

Hailey tested the marker, printing wobbly letters across the page. Ugly, but readable. "Deal," she said, and signed her name in giant orange loops.

Olivia laughed and took the notebook back. "I'll read you the notes in the car tomorrow too. Same seat, same time."

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
Gabriel sat in the waiting room of Dr. Okafor's office, pressing his thumb against the three new bumps along his jaw like they might flatten if he pushed hard enough. They didn't. Across from him, Noemi flipped through a magazine and then lowered it, studying him instead.

"You're doing the thing," she said. "The poking thing. Stop, my brother did that and it made everything worse."

"Made what worse?" Gabriel dropped his hands into his lap.

"The pimples, obviously." She held up the magazine, which had a diagram of skin with little arrows pointing into a pore. "I read this whole thing last month when mine started. Puberty hormones turn on the oil glands in your skin, and the glands make more of this stuff, it's called sebum, and it clogs your pores. That's where the pimples come from."

Gabriel leaned over to look. The diagram showed a hair follicle with a blob of oil stuck in it, and suddenly his whole face made sense. The bumps had started around his twelfth birthday, the same time his voice had gone squeaky in the middle of a class presentation. If hormones were behind his cracking voice, they were probably behind this too. Same invisible cause, different results.

"So if I can't see the hormones," he said slowly, "I can at least wash off the oil before it blocks anything."

"Obstructs," Noemi corrected. "The magazine says the sebum obstructs the pore. And washing helps, but don't scrub your face off."

When the nurse called his name, Gabriel went in for his sports physical, and he asked Dr. Okafor about the bumps before she even finished checking his reflexes. She nodded and said it was completely normal at his age, nothing permanent, and suggested a gentle face wash twice a day.

Afterward, in the pharmacy next door, Gabriel stood in the skincare aisle for ten minutes reading labels, and he finally picked a wash with the words "oil-control" on the front. Noemi gave it a thumbs-up from the end of the aisle. "See you Monday," she called, "with a face."

"Still going to have a face Monday either way," Gabriel said, and took the bottle to the cashier.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: By convention, a graph puts the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.
story:
Laurence stood in aisle seven of Hendrick's Hardware, holding two wooden dowels and a coiled spring, and tried to remember why she had decided to invest three whole weekends in a catapult. Her project, "Ramp Angle versus Launch Distance," had seemed simple until the launch distances stopped making any sense. The first four marble launches had gone farther as she raised the ramp. The fifth had plopped into the carpet two centimetres from the base. Something she couldn't see was messing with her results, and the science fair was in two days.

"Get the steel spring, not that plastic one," said Cash, who had tagged along because his mom was buying paint. "Plastic ones wear out. That could be your hidden thing."

"Maybe." Laurence turned the spring over. "Or maybe it's my ramp slipping between trials. I marked the angles with tape, but the clamp loosens."

At the register, they ran into Matthieu, who was buying sandpaper for his own project. He looked pale. "I have to rebuild my whole display board," he said. "I got your note, by the way. Thanks for nothing, it made my night worse."

The note had been about a graph. That morning Laurence had taped a message to his locker, because at lunch the day before she had glanced at his poster and felt something was off. She hadn't been able to say what.

Back home, she spread her data table across the kitchen table and read her own note again. "Matthieu, your graph looked backwards. I think you put ramp angle on the vertical axis, but isn't the thing you change supposed to go on the bottom? You'd better check. Laurence." She looked at her own draft graph, and her stomach dropped. She had done the exact same thing. Her ramp angle, the thing she chose in each trial, sat on the vertical axis, and her measured distances, the thing that depended on her choice, ran along the bottom. It looked like the distance decided the angle, which was upside down from how the experiment actually worked.

She called Cash. "On a graph, which axis does the independent variable go on?"

"The horizontal x-axis," he said, without hesitating. "The dependent variable goes on the vertical y-axis. Ms. Reddy made us chant it in September."

"Of course she did." Laurence hung up, erased her graph, and flipped the axes. When she plotted the points again, the weird fifth launch still sat low and lonely, but the rest climbed in a clean line, and that stray point now looked less like a mystery and more like a clue. She tightened the ramp clamp, picked up the marble, and launched it again.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Emergency agencies advise unplugging computers and other electronics during a power cut, because a surge of electricity when the power returns can damage them.
story:
Elizabeth was halfway through beating Layton at Monopoly when every light in the house went out at once.

"Hey!" Layton groaned into the darkness. "I was about to buy Park Place."

"No you weren't," Elizabeth said, feeling for the dice. "You had twelve dollars. I was counting."

They heard her mom in the kitchen, bumping into a chair and saying a word she probably hoped they didn't hear. A flashlight beam wobbled down the hall and found them at the coffee table, both still holding their money like the paper could glow.

"The whole street's out," her mom said. "Mrs. Nolan called from next door. She saw it go dark block by block, like dominoes."

They moved to the kitchen, where it was cooler, and ate cereal by flashlight because cereal, her mom claimed, was at least sort of nutritious. Layton disagreed. He argued that marshmallows canceled everything else out, and Elizabeth said that by his logic the box was dessert.

It was almost funny until Elizabeth remembered the desktop computer in the den, and her stomach dropped. Last spring, during a storm at her grandmother's house, the power had come back on with a jolt and fried the old radio on the counter. It had never worked again, even after Grandmother changed the batteries, which had made no sense to Elizabeth until she overheard the repairman say the word "surge" and describe electricity rushing back into anything still plugged in.

She set down her flashlight and went to the den, Layton trailing behind her. The screen was a dead black square. "We unplug them," she said, reaching behind the tower. "The computer, the console, everything. If the power comes back and they're plugged in, a surge can wreck them."

"So we're saving your stuff by sitting in the dark being bored," Layton said.

"We're saving my stuff by being smart in the dark. There's a difference." She found the console cord too, and the TV, coiling each one where she'd find it in the morning.

They played Monopoly by the front window instead, using the streetlight two houses over, which was somehow still on. Layton landed on her hotel and went bankrupt in nine minutes, a record he refused to celebrate.

At ten the lights blazed back on, all at once, and the microwave clock blinked 12:00. Elizabeth ran to the den. The computer sat unplugged, safe, its cord neatly coiled on the desk. She plugged it in, pressed the power button, and held her breath.

The screen lit up. She turned to Layton in the doorway.

"See? Genius."

"I see a girl who needs a better hobby than Monopoly," he said, and flipped the light switch off and on three times, just to hear it click.

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: Lifting the head forward to breathe makes the hips and legs sink, adding drag; turning the head to the side keeps the body flat.
story:
Hayden stood at the shallow end of the school pool, gripping the wall, watching Mustafa glide past like a shark with a schedule. Every time Hayden swam, the same thing happened: he lifted his head forward to grab air, and his legs sank like stones. He'd splash, sputter, and touch the bottom. Last week Ms. Bondarenko had timed his twenty-five metres at a laughable two minutes and something, and Ellis had announced it to the change room like a sports commentator. "Hayden breaches like a whale," Ellis had declared, "an exhausted whale."

Now, though, Hayden had a theory. He'd been watching Mustafa, who never seemed to tire, and he'd noticed something strange. Mustafa never looked forward when he breathed. His head turned to the side, one goggle out of the water, and his body stayed flat as a raft. Every time Hayden lifted his head forward, his hips dropped and his legs dragged low, like he was swimming uphill through wet cement. Maybe that was the whole problem. He didn't need more strength. He needed a different place to put his face.

"Watch this," he told Mustafa. "I'm going to try breathing to the side. If I stop looking up, maybe my legs stop sinking."

"Do it," Mustafa said. "If you touch bottom again, I'm starting a siege on your technique. Full siege. Water balloon at dawn."

Hayden pushed off. One arm, two arms, then he turned his head sideways and stole a breath, keeping one cheek pressed to the water. It felt like a sophisticated version of his old splashy stroke, quiet and smooth. His legs stayed near the surface. He took another side breath, then another, and the far wall came at him faster than it ever had.

"Time!" Ellis shouted, jabbing the stopwatch.

Ms. Bondarenko squinted at it. "Fifty-eight seconds."

Mustafa hauled Hayden up by the wrist. "A whale no more!"

"More like a very fast seal," Hayden said, and dove back under before anyone could argue.

activity: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
knowledge_domain: performing on stage for the first time in a school concert
fact: The squeal of microphone feedback happens when sound from a loudspeaker goes back into the microphone, gets amplified again, and loops louder and louder.
story:
Piper stood backstage holding her flute like it might bolt for the exit. The gym smelled like floor wax and nervous kids, and through the curtain she could see rows of folding chairs filling up. In ten minutes the spring concert would start, and her trio was first in the instrumental category, which meant no warm-up act between her and three hundred eyes.

Then the whistle began. Mr. Sok, who was running the sound system, had switched on a microphone for the announcer, and a piercing squeal ripped through the gym. Kids in the front rows covered their ears. He switched it off, switched it on again, and the squeal came back, worse, until somebody's baby brother started crying. "Not this," Piper whispered. Reid, waiting beside her with his trumpet, shrugged. "Maybe the mic is broken."

Piper didn't think so. She watched Mr. Sok drag the microphone stand toward the stage, and she noticed something. The closer he carried it to the tall loudspeaker at the edge of the stage, the louder the whistle got. She had learned about feedback last month, when her cousin's guitar amp did the same thing. The sound from the loudspeaker was going back into the microphone, getting amplified again, and looping louder and louder. It wasn't broken. It was trapped in a circle.

"Mr. Sok!" she called, stepping halfway onto the stage. "Point the microphone away from the speaker. The sound's looping back into it." He turned the stand so the mic faced the middle of the gym instead, and the whistle faded to nothing. He gave her a thumbs up. "Thank you, Piper. We'd have been here all night."

The announcer's voice came through clean and robust, and when the curtain opened, Piper walked out with Reid and Zakaria and played the first note of their piece. It wobbled only a little. Afterward, backstage, Zakaria grinned and said, "You fixed the whole concert before it even started." Piper laughed, still shaking, and started wiping down her flute.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Zack had one job at the cultural festival: find the ramen stall run by Yassine's family and bring back four bowls to the community table where his dad was saving seats. He carried the cardboard tray carefully, weaving past a drum circle and a booth selling beaded bracelets, because one tilt would send the broth everywhere and his dad had warned him twice already.

Back at the table, Yassine's grandmother pressed her palms together and gave a small bow, so Zack copied her, palms together, and bowed back a little too deep, nearly dunking his sleeve in the soup. Yassine grinned. "That's how we greet people at home," he said. "You're getting better."

Then came the problem. Everyone lifted their chopsticks, and around Zack the whole family began to slurp, loud and long, noodles vanishing behind cupped hands. Zack froze. At his house, slurping was the fastest signal that you had terrible manners, and his dad would give him the look across the dinner table. He stared into his bowl, unsure whether to eat quietly and seem rude for not joining in, or slurp and seem rude for the noise. There had to be a rule underneath this, and he meant to find it.

So he ran a test. He slurped one noodle, watching sideways. Nobody flinched. He slurped three more, louder. Yassine's grandmother nodded at him, pleased, and said something to Yassine in Japanese. "She says you eat like us," Yassine translated, laughing. "Slurping ramen is good manners in Japan. It's fine." Zack exhaled and slurped away, and his dad, after a hesitant start, did too.

That night Zack wrote a message to his friend Lianna, who had missed the festival because of a soccer game. "You should have seen it. I thought everyone was being gross, but it turned out to be polite. Tomorrow at lunch, want to recount the whole festival over noodles? I'll show you. Just don't tell your mom." Lianna's reply buzzed back within a minute: "Deal. Slurping contest, you and me. Loser buys the drinks."

Zack set his phone down, still smiling, and practiced one more long slurp into his cereal bowl.

"Mom," he called, "we're out of milk."

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A message sent in a private chat can be screenshotted and shared by anyone who receives it, so a private message is only as private as the people who read it.
story:
Tyler slumped into the desk chair, its synthetic fabric squeaking under him, and opened the group chat for the science project. Seven messages in, Hawa had posted a screenshot. It showed a private chat between Tyler and one other person, and in it Tyler had written that Celia's ideas were "slow" and that he wished he had a different partner. His stomach dropped. He had sent that message to exactly one classmate, in a private chat with a lock icon on it, three days ago.

Celia was already typing in the group. "wow. ok." Then, "meet me at the project table tomorrow i guess." Tyler stared at the screenshot until the letters blurred. The lock icon was still visible in the corner of the image. A private chat, he thought, and yet here it was, sitting in a group with eleven people in it. He began to infer what must have happened: the classmate he had sent it to must have taken a screenshot and passed it on, because a private chat could only be seen by the people in it until one of them decided to share it. The message hadn't leaked by magic. It had been handed along by a person.

He tested the idea quietly. He scrolled the group and found the classmate's name in the list of members. He checked their own private chat, and the exact words matched, down to the misspelling of "partener." Nobody else had ever seen that thread. It had to be that person. Tyler typed, deleted, typed again, and finally wrote in the group: "Celia, can you call me?" She sent a number.

"Your ideas aren't slow," he said when she picked up, his voice steadier than he expected. "I was frustrated about the deadline, not about you. That was a rude thing to write and I'm sorry." There was a pause, and he could hear a kettle whistling somewhere in her kitchen. "Okay," Celia said. "But how did it even get out there?" Tyler explained what he had worked out: a private chat was only private as long as everyone who read it kept it that way, and anyone who received a message could screenshot it and pass it anywhere. "So it's really about trust," Celia said slowly. "Yeah," Tyler said. "That's why I'm calling instead of typing it."

The next morning he arrived early and taped a note to the project table, next to the class constitution poster that Mr. Gallagher had everyone sign in September. The note read, "Celia leads the presentation. She had the best idea." When Celia walked in and read it, she sat down, opened her notebook, and slid the lava-lamp diagram across the table toward him. "Page two," she said. "We still need a real volcano."

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The folding chairs squeaked every time someone shifted, and the gymnasium smelled like floor wax and old basketballs. Gabrielle sat on the stage between Lucas and a girl from another school, holding her number card so tightly that the corners bent. She had been diligent about studying, two hundred words a night, but she knew that wasn't the same as being ready, because a spelling bee could always reach into a pocket you hadn't checked.

Her moment came in the third round. Mr. Sadeghi, who was reading the words, adjusted his glasses and said, "Your word is 'schema.' It begins with the sound 'sk.'" Then he added, as he was supposed to, "Language of origin: Greek."

Gabrielle's mind went briefly, completely blank. She knew what a schema was, a kind of pattern or framework, but the beginning was the problem. In English that sound could be spelled all sorts of ways. Then something Alia had told her at lunch floated up, half buried under a memory of a sandwich. Alia had missed "chef" at the classroom bee because she'd spelled the "sh" sound with "ch," and she'd come back to the table muttering that French used "ch" for "sh." If French used "ch" for "sh," then Greek must use "ch" for "k," like in "chorus." So a Greek word starting with the "k" sound would start with "ch." It was a guess built on one data point, and she had about four seconds to decide whether to trust it.

"Could I have the definition?" she asked, mostly to buy time. Mr. Sadeghi said it was a framework or organized pattern, and she nodded as if this were news. In the front row, Lucas gave her a thumbs up so enormous it looked like he was hailing a taxi. Somewhere behind him a small child dropped an entire bag of popcorn, which was either an omen or just a hungry kid. "S-c-h-e-m-a," Gabrielle said. "Schema." The bell of Mr. Sadeghi's pause lasted one long second, and then he said, "Correct."

She went on to finish second overall, undone in the end by "tracheotomy," which, she learned afterward, was also Greek, and would also have started with "c-h" if she had thought one more step down the road she'd discovered. Alia found her by the water fountain. "You used the French thing," Alia said. "I saw your face change."

"I did," Gabrielle admitted. "I have no idea how to spell anything anymore. Every word might be secretly Greek." They walked out through the double doors, and Alia held up her phone showing the word "chorus," with "Greek" written under it in her notes. "So from now on," Alia said, "we assume everything is Greek and conceal our panic." Gabrielle laughed so hard she bumped into the trophy table, and the second-place medal swung against her chest like it was congratulating itself.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: In 2021, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee.
story:
Aria pressed her palms flat on her desk while Ms. Balogun called the spelling bee to order. Twenty-three kids sat in rows, but only two of them would go to the regionals, and she had wanted one of those spots ever since September. "Round one," Ms. Balogun announced. "Linden."

Linden stood, squared his shoulders, and spelled "crepuscular" without a single pause. Aria's stomach dropped. She had found that word on the very last page of the practice list, buried among the hardest ones, and she had spent her weekend memorizing page after page because she believed Ms. Balogun saved the monsters for the final rounds. She tested her idea all morning, keeping a tally in her notebook: easy words first, harder words later, the last page last. So far the tally held.

She survived "dossier" and "anemone." In round five, Rowan went down on "zhuzh," and Linden got "quixotic" right, so it was just the two of them. Aria's hand trembled a little as she spelled "contradiction," a word she knew well because it described the two voices in her head: one said she could win the regionals, the other said champions never looked like her. On Saturday, at the library, she had checked that second voice against the shelves of bee records. In 2021, she had read, Zaila Avant-garde became the first African-American contestant to win the Scripps National Spelling Bee. Aria had copied the page number into her notebook and read it three times before the librarian asked if she needed help finding anything else.

"Final round," said Ms. Balogun. "Aria. Your word is 'immune.'" Aria asked for the definition, asked for the language of origin, and bought herself four seconds to think. Then she noticed something in her tally that refuted her whole theory: the final word had come from the middle of the list, not the end. Ms. Balogun had mixed the pages. All that page-by-page memorizing had been aimed at a pattern that did not exist, and yet here she stood, still standing, because she had also drilled the middle pages her father had quizzed her on for fun.

"I, M, M, U, N, E," she said.

"That is correct," said Ms. Balogun, and Linden let out a breath and applauded louder than anyone. "And Linden, as runner-up, you join her at the regionals." Linden leaned over from the next row. "I thought you'd be worried the whole time," he whispered. "I was, at first," Aria whispered back. "Then I read about a champion named Zaila Avant-garde and stopped worrying about the wrong things." She closed her notebook, and on the cover, in careful letters, she had already written her new plan: middle pages first.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
knowledge_domain: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
fact: Pencils marked H have more clay and make lighter, harder marks, while pencils marked B have more graphite and make softer, darker marks.
story:
Connor pressed so hard on his pencil that the paper squeaked, and the shadow under his sphere still looked like a smudge of dust. Across the table, Elia held up her own drawing, which had the same problem, a pale, weak shadow that would never convince anyone.

"Mine looks like the light source gave up halfway," she said. She squinted at her pencil. "It says 2H. What does the H even mean?"

Mr. Smith, walking past with his coffee mug, paused long enough to say, "Try the other tin," and kept going, because Mr. Smith believed in making people figure things out.

Connor dug through the second tin and found a pencil marked 4B. He tapped it on his palm. "H, B. H, B." He drew one slow stroke with each on the corner of his paper. The H stroke came out light and thin, like a whisper. The B stroke came out soft and dark, like a bruise on a plum.

"Okay, okay," he said, holding them up. "The H pencil is an herbivore. It nibbles, politely. The B pencil is predatory. It attacks the page and leaves a big dark mark."

"That is the silliest thing you've ever said," said Elia, but she was already grabbing a B pencil. She shaded the shadow under her sphere in two careful passes, and this time it looked like a real shadow, not a rumor of one.

"The B pencils must have more graphite," Connor said slowly, watching his own dark shadow bloom, "and the H ones have more clay, so they're harder and lighter." He tested it once more to clarify, laying an H line next to a B line. Sure enough. He added the cast shadow stretching to the right, away from the lamp, and a small white highlight where the light hit the top of the sphere.

Elia tilted her drawing toward the window. "My sphere finally looks round instead of like a flat cookie."

Connor signed his name in the corner, using, of course, the B pencil.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French uses the verb "avoir" (to have) to give age: "J'ai douze ans" means "I am twelve," but word for word says "I have twelve years."
story:
The festival smelled like fried plantains and cinnamon, and somewhere behind the folding tables a drum circle had started up. Marcus stood at his school's French booth with a stack of flashcards, waiting for visitors. His whole presentation was about describing his family: his mother, his grandmother, his little sister, and Buckwheat, the world's laziest beagle. He had written it out on index cards, and the work had been tedious, checking every adjective twice, but tonight it had to sound natural.

"Je me présente," he began when the first family wandered over. "J'ai un chien. Il s'appelle Buckwheat. Il est petit et paresseux." That part went fine. Then he got to himself. "Je suis douze ans," he said, "et j'ai une petite soeur." A girl about his age squinted at him like he'd said something weird, but she only shrugged and moved on toward the food tents.

After the crowd thinned, Marcus found a bench and pulled out his phone. He'd texted Brantley, who had finished French last year, an hour ago, and finally a message buzzed back: "dude. suis = am. you can't BE twelve years, you HAVE them. J'ai douze ans. it means I am twelve but word for word it says I have twelve years. weird but that's the rule. check your other sentences too." Marcus read it three times. If age worked that way, maybe other things did too. He thought about the pattern: French kept using "have" where English used "be." His cards said "J'ai les cheveux noirs," which he had memorized without thinking, and that was "I have black hair." Hair was in the have category too. He flipped through every card, hunting for any other place he'd used the wrong verb, and fixed each one in pencil.

He persevered through the last stack even when the drums got loud and Harlan waved at him from the puppet show across the grass. When Mr. Littlechild, his neighbor, ambled up to the booth for the second time that evening, Marcus took a breath.

"Je m'appelle Marcus. J'ai douze ans," he said, steady and clear. "J'ai un chien. Il s'appelle Buckwheat."

Mr. Littlechild clapped slowly, like Marcus had scored a goal. "Now that," he said, "sounds like a language."

Marcus grinned and turned his flashcards face down, all except one, the one with Buckwheat's floppy ears drawn in the corner, which he slid across the table for Mr. Littlechild to keep.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: Mandarin Chinese puts a measure word between a number and a noun: "one cat" is "yì zhī māo," where "zhī" is the measure word used for many animals.
story:
Asher pressed his phone against the window of his grandmother's apartment in Taipei, filming the scooters flashing by below. Tomorrow he would narrate a video for his class back home, all in Mandarin, introducing his family and their pets. His friend Sirine had begged him to do it. "You're actually there," she had said on the call last night, bouncing so hard her pigtails blurred. "Nobody else can show a real street. I'll hold the camera at school, I just need you to actually say the words."

The problem was the words. Asher had practiced in the mirror that morning: Wo jia you san mao, three cats, we have three. It sounded fine to him. But when he said it to his grandmother at breakfast, she laughed behind her hand and shook her head, and he had no idea why. The tones? He checked each one twice. Maybe his mouth was doing something wrong in the middle of the sentence, some sound hiding where he couldn't hear it.

At lunch, the smell of scallion pancakes filled the tiny kitchen, crispy and hot, and his grandmother set down a plate with steam still rising off it. "Nutritious," she said in English, one of her favorite words, tapping the egg inside. Asher barely touched his food. He was too busy thinking. He said the sentence again, slow, and this time his grandmother leaned close. "San," she said, holding up three fingers, "zhī," and then she made a cat with her hands, whiskers in the air. "Sān zhī māo."

There it was. A whole word, zhī, stuck right between the number and the animal, and he had been walking straight past it the entire time. His grandmother hadn't been laughing at his tones at all. He grabbed his notebook and wrote it down before it could escape, then tested the idea out loud. Liàng zhī māo? His grandmother nodded. Yì zhī māo? She nodded again, beaming.

Then came the twist. A scratching sounded at the door, and something small and furry trotted in, tail thumping. The neighbor's dog, who visited every afternoon. Asher pointed, heart pounding, and tried his new word on a brand-new animal. "Yì zhī gǒu," he said, and held his breath.

"Duì," his grandmother said. Correct. It worked for dogs too. Asher jumped up so fast his chair scraped the floor, and he filmed the dog on the balcony in the golden afternoon light, saving the clip for Sirine, whispering the sentence twice more so he wouldn't lose it before morning.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscles grow stronger during recovery after training, not during the workout itself, so rest days are part of getting better.
story:
Jayden pressed his palm against the gym wall and counted the seconds until the pain in his legs faded. Twelve. At Saturday's game it had been sixteen. He watched Tobin sprint across the community center floor, easy as anything, and felt the small tight knot in his chest get tighter.

"You're slower every week," Tobin said after drills, dribbling the ball in lazy circles. "You were faster than me in October. Now I beat you every single race."

"Thanks for the update," Jayden said. Jazmin sat down beside them, unwrapping a granola bar she'd been saving since lunch.

"Coach doesn't permit food on the court," she said, but she kept eating it, crumbs and all. "I've been timing you two, by the way. Jayden, your sprint times went up for three weeks straight. Tobin's stayed flat, and he skips Tuesdays."

Jayden frowned. He practiced every day the center was open, even Sundays, even the day after games when his legs felt like wet sand. Tobin came four days and rested the rest. It made no sense, unless resting was doing something. He turned the idea over the way you'd turn over a puzzle piece: muscles getting stronger not during practice, but in the quiet days after, when he wasn't using them at all. It sounded backwards. But his slowest weeks had come right after his hardest ones, and that fit.

"I'm taking Sunday off," he announced. "And Thursday. Science experiment."

"You're going to get slower by sitting around," Tobin said, grinning. "Also, my dad says if your legs fall off, that's not covered under warranty."

"My legs are not a toaster, Tobin."

Two weeks later, on a gray afternoon with rain ticking against the high windows, Jayden lined up against Tobin at the baseline. Jazmin stood at the wall with her phone raised like a starting flag, her symmetrical ponytails perfectly even, which she claimed improved her accuracy. "On three," she called. "One, two, three."

They exploded down the court, and for the first time all season Jayden's legs felt like springs instead of sand. He touched the far line a half step ahead.

"Rematch," Tobin panted. "Sunday. Both of us."

"Sunday's a rest day," Jayden said. "Monday."

Tobin groaned, then bumped his fist anyway. "Monday. You're buying the granola bars."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: When ecologist Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels from a stretch of Washington State shore, mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species.
story:
Landon sat on an overturned bucket in the corner of the barn, his sketchpad balanced on his knee. The assignment from Mr. Weiss was to draw a food chain starting with the sun and ending with a top predator, and then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. He had started with a tundra chain, because he liked drawing caribou, but halfway through the wolf he had stopped. He didn't actually know what would happen if the wolf vanished, and guessing felt like cheating.

While the others were out at the pumpkin field with Loukas and Lilith, Landon wandered past the feed shelves and found a stack of old nature magazines. One had a photo of a rocky shore on the cover. He flipped through it and found a story about an ecologist named Robert Paine who had worked on a stretch of Washington State shore. Paine had removed a starfish that ate mussels, just to see what would happen. After that, the mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species. Landon read the paragraph twice, then copied the names into the margin of his sketchpad.

"So one predator keeps everything else alive," he said out loud to the empty barn.

He wanted to test the idea before he trusted it. Behind the farmhouse there was a small creek pool where a heron stalked minnows every morning. Landon walked there now, crouched on the flat stone Lilith had shown him last autumn, and counted what he could see: minnows, snails, a knot of green algae, one crayfish. Then he walked to a second pool upstream, narrow and shaded, where no heron could stand, and counted again. The algae there grew in a thick mat across the whole surface, and he saw only two minnows and no snails at all.

He sat down right there with his pad and began a second drawing, arrows and all. When the class gathered back at the wagon, he turned the page toward Loukas. "Look," Landon said. "Sun, algae, minnows, heron. And here's the pool without the heron." He tapped the shaded drawing with his pencil. "The algae just takes over."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
knowledge_domain: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
fact: Singing in unison means everyone sings the same notes; singing in harmony means different parts sing different notes at the same time.
story:
Everly stood in the music room with the rest of the choir, clutching her folder like it might float away. Ms. Lee had split the group in half, and Everly's half was learning a brand new part while the others sang the tune they already knew. When they tried the tune alone, it sounded fine but thin, like a drawing done in one pencil stroke. Everly couldn't figure out why the same song suddenly needed two different lines of notes, and it bothered her all through warm-up, the way a skipped word bothers you in a book.

"I keep sliding into your notes," she admitted to Daphne at the piano during break. Daphne was in the other half, the one singing the tune. "Every time you start, my part slips away like I never learned it." Everly stared at the keyboard and tried an experiment. She played the tune's first three notes, then added her own part underneath, watching her fingers. Different keys, pressed at the same time. She played the tune's notes alone, then both sets together, and the sound that came out was fuller, rounder, like the difference between a sketch and a painting.

"Wait," Everly said, and called Andrea and two others over. "I think I get it. When we all sang the same notes before, that was unison, and it sounded thin. Harmony means different parts sing different notes at the same time. That's why the song needs both of us." She played the two sets of notes again, one stacked on the other, and watched their faces change.

They tried it standing in the middle of the room. The first run wobbled badly, and Everly cracked up laughing when she caught herself following Daphne's line again. "Plug your ears," Daphne suggested, and Everly tried singing with one finger pressed against her ear so she could hear her own part better. It helped. On the next run, the two parts held against each other, and the room filled with a sound that was nothing like the thin, arid single line from before. Everly grinned across at Daphne and sang her part louder.

After practice, she helped Ms. Lee stack the chairs, humming both lines at once all the way to the bus loop, where her mother waited after her long commute home from the city. "Which part is that?" her mother asked through the window. Everly smiled and sang the other one.

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: When the Nile flood went down, it left a layer of dark, fertile mud on the fields, which is why Egyptians called their land Kemet, the black land.
story:
Connor had a problem, and the problem was sitting on his desk in a plastic bag: a scoop of dirt from the backyard. Tomorrow he had to explain to his class why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming, and so far all he had were three half-finished notes and a doodle of a cat wearing a pharaoh hat.

Lila had said the dirt would help. "My grandpa says the best tomatoes come from the darkest soil," she'd told him at lunch, holding up her sandwich like it was evidence. "Try it."

So Connor tried it. He lined up two pots on the kitchen windowsill, one with dark soil from the shady corner by the fence, one with pale, dusty dirt from near the sidewalk, and pushed a bean seed into each. Then he paced around the kitchen, because pacing felt like thinking.

"Why do you keep walking in circles?" his dad asked, peering over a crossword.

"I'm figuring out Egypt."

"Ah. Carry on."

Connor flopped onto the couch and stared at his notes. Kings wanted big tombs. Okay, but why there? Why that spot, why that river? He grabbed his pencil and drew a map of Egypt from memory, which looked like a bent noodle. He drew the Nile down the middle. Then he stopped. The river. The river did something every year, he remembered, something that had to do with the fields.

"Think, Connor," he muttered. "The river. The flood. What happens when a flood goes down?"

He looked at the window, where rain from yesterday still streaked the glass, and where mud from the yard had dried in a brown smear on the sill. Mud. A flood that goes down leaves mud behind. He lunged for his laptop and typed fast.

He was still reading when Lila and Marlowe arrived after dinner, supposedly to "study." Marlowe went straight to the fridge. "Your bean experiment is rigged," Lila said, tapping the pots. "That one's got, what, synthetic plant food in it?"

"No, that's the point, no shortcuts. Dark dirt versus sad dirt. Grandpa's rule."

"And here's my rule," Marlowe said through a mouthful of leftovers. "Never trust a noodle map." He held up Connor's Egypt drawing.

"That noodle is my pyramid explanation. Watch." Connor pointed at the map. "Every year the Nile flooded, and when the flood went down, it left a layer of dark, fertile mud on the fields. That's why Egyptians called their land Kemet."

"Kemet," Marlowe repeated. "Sounds like a cough syrup."

"It means the black land," Connor said. "My bean pot proves it, sort of. Dark soil, better plants. The flood was like the whole country's planting season arriving in one go. Tons of food means you can feed workers, builders, whoever's on top of the hierarchy, instead of everyone having to farm all day. Extra food, extra people, extra hands. Pyramids."

Lila squinted at the windowsill. "So the guy who invented the pyramid was basically standing on old mud."

"Standing on Kemet," Connor said. "The black land."

Marlowe raised his juice glass. "To mud. The real genius of Egypt."

Connor grinned and wrote one last note: the beans will confirm. Tomorrow, the class wouldn't know what hit them. He set both pots square in the morning sun.

activity: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
knowledge_domain: to create a strong password and explain why the same one should not be reused
fact: The US standards agency NIST says a password that is the only thing protecting an account should be at least 15 characters long.
story:
Oliver sat cross-legged on the living room rug with his tablet, because the sign-up screen for the game site refused to go any further without a password. Behind him, his dad was elbow-deep in the plumbing under the sink, and every so often a wrench clanged against a pipe. Oliver typed his usual password, the one he used for everything, and the little bar beside it turned green.

"Eight characters," said Mouhamed, leaning over his shoulder. "You can do better than that."

Mouhamed wanted to be a game tester someday, and he read about computer stuff the way other kids read about football. "My cousin works with computers," he went on. "He told me the US standards agency NIST says a password that is the only thing protecting an account should be at least 15 characters long."

"Eight was fine for my old account," Oliver said, but even as he said it, he remembered last spring, when someone got into his video account and deleted every saved level. He had never found out how. Maybe someone had guessed it, or maybe the same password had leaked from somewhere else, since he used it everywhere. It was like deducing where a leak came from by following the drip: you couldn't see the cause, only the puddle. He couldn't see who had taken his account, but the pattern pointed at the one password he reused again and again.

He deleted what he had typed and started over, picking four random words strung together until the count on the screen read fifteen, then sixteen. The bar turned green in a deeper shade this time, as if it meant it. "Every account gets its own," he said. "Even if it's annoying."

"Smart," said Mouhamed, grinning, and his grin was infectious. Oliver caught himself smiling too, tablet balanced on his knees, while under the sink his dad gave one last heroic twist and the pipe went quiet.

"There," his dad called out, wiping his hands. "Now nobody's getting through that either."

activity: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
knowledge_domain: going to a first sleepover at a friend's house
fact: Since January 1, 2023, U.S. law has listed nine major food allergens, including peanuts, milk, eggs and sesame, which must be declared on packaged food labels.
story:
Piper unrolled her sleeping bag in Selina's backyard tent and set her flashlight beside it, like a tiny lighthouse on the carpet of grass. It was her first real sleepover, and she had packed three days early, which Gus said was ridiculous, but Gus wasn't allergic to sesame, so Gus could pack late if he wanted. He lived next door and had been invited for the pizza part of the evening, and he had already eaten half the bowl of pretzels.

"Before we order, does anyone have food allergies?" Selina's mom called from the back door. "We're checking everything tonight."

"Sesame," Piper said. "And I always check anyway."

Gus leaned over the pretzel bag, suddenly interested. "You ate four of those."

"I know," Piper said, and her stomach did a slow, cold flip. She picked up the bag and turned it to the ingredient list. Since January 1, 2023, she had learned, the law listed nine major food allergens, and packaged food labels had to declare them. Peanuts, milk, eggs, sesame, all nine of them, spelled out right there on the package. That was the rule she trusted more than anyone's memory, including her own. She ran her finger down the tiny print, past "flour" and "salt," and there it was, plain as anything: sesame.

She put the bag down carefully, as if it might bite. "Gus. Those have sesame. In the ingredients."

Gus stopped chewing. "You're kidding."

"I'm not." Piper showed him the line, and he read it twice, his eyebrows climbing. Her heart was knocking, but she thought it through the way her doctor had taught her: she had eaten maybe five pretzels, and so far her lips weren't tingling and her throat felt normal. It could take a while, though, so she told Selina's mom everything, honestly, including the exact count. Selina's mom already had her phone out and the antihistamine from Piper's backpack, and Piper drank water and sat very still while everyone hovered.

"I'm so sorry," Gus kept saying. "I handed you the bowl."

"I took them," Piper said. "But next time, help me check first. Deal?"

"Deal," Gus said, and he picked up every snack box in the tent and read each label out loud, hunting for the word sesame like a detective. Selina grabbed the popcorn bag, and Piper took the crackers. Between the three of them, they built a safe pile and a no pile, and Piper decided it was worth it to invest her whole evening in this one project, because knowing was better than guessing.

When the pizza came, sesame-free and steaming in its box, they ate it cross-legged in the tent with the flashlight glowing between them. Gus was already planning a second sleepover, in his yard this time, near the equator of the lawn where the grass was softest, he declared, and where it would be feasible to string up more lights. Selina said that wasn't what equator meant, and they argued happily about it while Piper took the last slice.

"Read the box one more time," she said, grinning, and held it up to the flashlight.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: Many shelf labels show a unit price, such as the price per litre, so different sizes can be compared; the bigger carton is often, but not always, cheaper per litre.
story:
Riley stood in the garage next to her mother's car, holding a five-dollar bill so tightly it crinkled. "Milk, two litres if you can, change comes back to me," her mother said, backing the car out. "You've got this." Riley had walked to the corner store before, but never alone, and her stomach did a slow flip as the car disappeared around the corner.

She thought about last summer, when her cousin had sent her to buy popsicles and she'd come back with the wrong kind and no receipt, and how her cousin's laugh had made her want to hide in the garage forever. That time still had the power to embarrass her, even months later. Not this time. She checked the money in her jacket pocket twice, then set off down the sidewalk, counting cracks to keep her mind busy.

At the store she found the milk cooler and stopped cold. There was one big two-litre carton and, beside it, small one-litre cartons. Two small ones would also be two litres. The big carton cost more than one small, but less than two. Which was better? She stared until her eyes found tiny print on the shelf label: a second price, labelled per litre. "Unit price," she whispered. She did the math with her finger on the freezer door, the way Ms. Moretti had made them practise mental arithmetic until it was automatic. The big carton's per-litre price was lower, so it was the better deal. She reached for it, then paused and checked the small carton's label too, just to be sure, because maybe the smaller one could win. It didn't. Big carton, lower price per litre. She carried it to the cashier like a trophy.
