Walking home, she noticed the carton's printed design had a kind of lopsided symmetry, one side mirroring the other except for a bright synthetic-looking sun on the left panel, and she laughed out loud at herself for inspecting a milk carton like a detective. At home she set the milk on the counter and counted the change into her mother's palm, coin by coin, all of it there. "Good milk?" her mother asked. Riley grinned. "Cheapest per litre on the whole shelf."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger, and in that case a person is actually required to eat or drink.
story:
Stella's stomach had been growling since the walk to the synagogue, but that was nothing compared with the pale look on her cousin's face. They were sitting in the back rows for the Yom Kippur service, the long day when their whole family fasted, and her cousin, who had diabetes and was used to the routine, kept closing his eyes between prayers.

Last year Stella had messed this up. She remembered offering him her water bottle in the parking lot and whispering that nobody would see, and he had shaken his head and gone hungry anyway, and by evening he had been so shaky that their aunt had driven him home early. Stella had felt terrible about it for weeks. This year she watched him the way other people watched the sky before rain, looking for a pattern she could act on.

During the break between services, she found the rabbi by the doorway. "My cousin looks really bad," she said. "But it's the fast, so what can we do?" The rabbi put a hand on her shoulder. "Jewish law waives the Yom Kippur fast when health is in danger," he said. "In that case a person is actually required to eat or drink." Stella blinked. Required, like a commandment, not just permitted.

She tested it against what she knew, turning it over like a puzzle piece. If it were merely allowed, her cousin would keep refusing, because he refused things that were merely allowed. If it were required, he would have to say yes. She filled a cup with juice, because his blood sugar dropping fast made him vulnerable to fainting, and carried it to him through the crowd of relatives who orbited the snack table nobody was touching.

"Drink this," she said. "The rabbi says you're required to." Her cousin stared at the cup, then at her, then drank the whole thing in four swallows.

Color came back into his face like a photograph developing. "You're going to tell me the rabbi keeps a database of people who get to eat on Yom Kippur," he said.

"Shh," Stella said. "I'm fasting."

activity: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
knowledge_domain: to understand the changes of puberty and why daily showers and deodorant matter
fact: Showering with soap, especially after exercise, washes away the sweat and bacteria that cause body odor.
story:
The bathroom mirror was fogged, and Levi wrote his name in it with his finger while he thought. Yesterday at practice he had run six laps, and today at school Jazlyn had slid her desk an inch away from his, and Lyana had fanned herself with a folder and said, "Whoa." Nobody had said the actual word, but Levi could put the clues together. Something invisible was happening, and he was the prime candidate for causing it.

He ran an experiment on the spot. He sniffed his shirt, gagged a little, and turned on the shower. Soap, hot water, scrub, dry off, and then the deodorant stick his mom had bought and left on the sink like a hint. He drew an invisible line under each armpit, then another, because one seemed shy.

On Monday he came to school clean after Saturday practice, because he had figured out the pattern: sweat itself was the start, but the smell came after, and it built up gradual, like a snowball rolling downhill. A shower with soap washed away the sweat and the bacteria that made the odor, especially right after exercise, when there was the most to wash off. So the rule he tested was simple. Shower right after practice, not two days later, and the snowball never got rolling.

At lunch Lyana leaned her chair closer to his, which was data. Then Jazlyn leaned in too and said, "New soap? You smell like a pine forest."

"Deodorant," Levi said. "Invisible kind."

Jazlyn held up her water bottle. "My brother uses that kind. It smells like the actual tree died for him."

"He wears too much," Levi said, feeling like an expert now. "You only need two lines."

Behind them, Mr. Cho paused on his way past their table, took a careful breath through his nose, and gave Levi a small nod, like a judge scoring a routine. Then he kept walking, carrying his coffee and his sandwich toward the far table, where the eighth graders sat. Levi watched him go, then turned back and slid the ketchup toward Lyana before she even asked.

activity: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
knowledge_domain: to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature
fact: In Westminster-style legislatures such as Canada's and the United Kingdom's, first reading introduces a bill and has it printed without debate.
story:
The courthouse basement smelled of dust and old coffee, and Sebastian's class had claimed three rows of folding chairs in front of a borrowed TV cart. They were there for a field trip about civic buildings, but Ms. Mercado had switched the channel to the legislature channel, and now nobody was looking at the marble staircases upstairs.

On the screen, a member stood up, dropped a paper on the clerk's table, and sat down again. The Speaker said the bill would be read a first time and printed, and then everything moved on. Sebastian blinked. It had lasted maybe eight seconds. "That can't be it," he whispered to Joanne. "Where's the arguing?"

"That's first reading," said Norman, leaning over from the next chair. "It just introduces the bill and gets it printed. There's no debate at all yet."

Joanne frowned. "No debate? Then what was all that stuff about the landlord bill taking months?"

Sebastian thought about that. If the first step took seconds, the months had to live somewhere else, in the stages he hadn't seen. He imagined the bill as a runner passing a baton: introduced, printed, and only then fought over. It was like the maple tree outside his window, he thought; you never saw the roots invade the drain pipe, you only saw the wet patch on the basement floor. The slow part was hidden. He'd skipped a whole month of social studies in the fall, back when he'd decided reading was easier than listening, and this felt like the bill for that choice arriving now.

He raised his hand. "Ms. Mercado, if we watch, will we see the next part?"

"We'll see the start of second reading," she said. "Watch what changes."

On the screen, another member rose, and this time she spoke. She spoke for a long time, and another member stood to answer her, and the Speaker had to call for order. Sebastian leaned forward so hard the folding chair creaked.

"There it is," Joanne murmured. "The months."

Norman grinned. "Eight seconds to introduce it, and then all this."

Sebastian pulled his notebook out and drew a little track with a baton on it, first box tiny, second box huge. Under the first box he wrote "first reading, no debate." Then he looked up at the screen, where two members were now talking over each other, and he kept his pencil hovering, waiting to see what filled the third.

activity: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
knowledge_domain: to write a Python loop that prints the times table for any number the user types
fact: A Python for loop runs its indented block once for each value, so for i in range(1, 11) runs the multiplication line ten times.
story:
Ella sat cross-legged on the rug in Lorelei's basement, balancing Lorelei's laptop on her knees while the dryer hummed behind the wall. Lorelei wanted a program for her little brother's math practice, and she wanted it by Friday so he could drill before his quiz. Ella had typed ten lines in a row, each one printing a multiple of seven, and it worked, but it looked wrong to her somehow, like a paragraph made of the same sentence copied over and over.

"You realize," said Danika from the old couch, where she was braiding a jump rope into knots, "that you're being very gullible about your own code. It runs once and you trust it forever." Ella ran the program again anyway, because testing was the only way to be sure. The output marched down the screen, 7 times 1 is 7, 7 times 2 is 14, all the way to 7 times 10 is 70. It worked. But Lorelei's brother might want the eights next week, and the nines after that, and Ella did not want to type ten new lines every single time. That was the real problem, and she chewed the end of her ponytail while she stared at it.

She remembered the green sticky note on Mr. Chanthavong's classroom door, the one with for i in range(1, 11) written on it. She had walked past it every day for a month without understanding it. Now she inferred, from the way her own ten lines repeated, that the sticky note meant the indented line underneath got run once for each value, which would be ten times. One multiplication line, then, could do the work of ten. She deleted her copied lines and typed the loop, with a single print line indented under it, and asked the user for a number first.

"Objection," Danika said, pointing at the screen like a lawyer. "The defendant claims her loop is magic." Ella pressed Enter, typed 8, and watched the eights march down the screen, one line for each value, all ten of them, exactly right. Lorelei leaned over her shoulder and smiled. "Do the twelves," she said. Ella typed 12 and hit Enter.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A pet microchip has no GPS and cannot track where an animal is; it only gives its ID number when a scanner is held close.
story:
The cardboard carrier on the passenger seat wobbled every time the bus braked, and Henry put a steadying hand on it the whole ride home from the veterinary clinic. Inside was a gray kitten with a shaved patch on her shoulder where Ms. Mehta, the vet, had just placed a microchip. Henry had asked whether he could watch her on his phone afterward, like a dot on a map, and Ms. Mehta had smiled and said the chip only gave an ID number when a scanner was held close to it. It had no GPS and could not track where an animal was. Henry had nodded, but he hadn't really believed her until he opened the app and found nothing but a registration form.

Flashback to that morning: the waiting room had smelled like antiseptic and dog. Dominick had come along because his own cat, Biscuit, had been missing for nine days. "She's chipped," Dominick kept saying. "My dad says they'll find her." Raphael, flipping through a poster about parasites, said the whole class agreed, and Henry had been part of that consensus too, nodding along. Then a technician came out with Biscuit herself, scratched and thin, in a towel. A neighbor three streets over had caught her and brought her in, and the scanner had beeped out Biscuit's ID number from the chip, and that was how Dominick got the call. Nobody had tracked anything. A person had found her, and the chip had only told them whose cat she was.

That evening, Henry sat on his bedroom floor with the kitten and thought about how Biscuit had been found. The chip hadn't magnified her location at all; it was more like a name tag hidden under the skin, silent until a scanner woke it up. He tested the idea anyway. He carried the kitten to the far side of the room, checked his phone, and saw only his own reflection in the dark screen. Then he called Dominick.

"So your dad was wrong," Henry said. "The chip can't tell anyone where she is. It only says who she is when somebody's already holding her."

"That's what Raphael figured out too," Dominick said. "He printed maps anyway. He wants to hang them up at school tomorrow, like they did for that extinct breed poster, so people know what Biscuit looks like and can call if they spot her again. She's home now, but she got out once, so."

Henry looked at the kitten chewing the strap of his backpack. "Tell Raphael I'll bring the carrier," he said. "If she gets out, we don't wait for a beep. We go look."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Salt water makes iron rust faster than fresh water, which is one reason cars rust more in places that salt their roads in winter.
story:
Tristan set two jars on his grandfather's workbench and dropped a plain iron nail into each one. "This one gets tap water," he said, "and this one gets salt water." Andi leaned over the jars with her phone, ready to take the first photo for their science fair board.

The problem was the deadline. The fair was in two weeks, and nothing had happened to either nail by Friday. "We could just write an approximate answer," Andi said, scrolling through their notes. "Like, 'rusting takes a while.'" Tristan shook his head. Mr. Becker had already told him his last project failed because it had no evidence, only guesses, and he was not going through that again in front of the whole gym.

His grandfather came in from the driveway carrying a bag of ice melt. "Need anything from the hardware store?" he asked. Tristan looked at the bag, then at the jars. "Grandpa, why do you put that stuff on the driveway?" "So I don't break my hip," his grandfather said. Tristan frowned. His dad had complained last month that the family car looked older than it was, ever since they moved here. "The salt on the roads," his dad had said, half to himself, "it eats the car." Tristan had thought that sounded like complaining about the recession eating everything else. Now he wondered whether it was literally true.

He typed it into Andi's phone. She read the screen out loud. "Cars rust more in places that salt their roads in winter." Tristan tapped the salt-water jar. "Because salt water makes iron rust faster than fresh water. That's what we're testing, and the internet says we're right." Andi frowned at the clear liquid in both jars. "Nothing's happening in there, though. It's been four days." Tristan picked up the tap-water jar and studied it. He could not see any change at all. Maybe the salt jar was ahead and the tap jar was just slow, or maybe both were doing nothing. There was only one way to find out, and it was to wait.

By the following Friday, the answer had appeared without asking permission. The nail in the salt water was rough and orange-brown along its whole length, and the water itself had turned the color of weak tea. The tap-water nail showed only a few dark patches near the head. Andi lined up the photos in order on the board. "Physical change, chemical change," she said, writing the two labels. "Melting ice is physical, because it's still water. Rusting is a chemical change, because the iron turns into something else entirely. It doesn't turn back." Tristan peeled a flake of rust off the salt-water nail with his thumbnail, and it crumbled like dried mud.

At the fair, a judge stopped at their board and pointed at the two photos. "So which jar proves what?" Tristan picked up the salt-water nail in its plastic bag and held it next to the gray one. "This one was in salt water," he said. "Grandpa's car would rust faster than a car in a place that never salts its roads, even if both cars were the same age. Same iron, same water in the sky, just different water on the road."

activity: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
knowledge_domain: to swim twenty-five metres front crawl with side breathing
fact: Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races because it is the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes.
story:
The community centre had two halves, a hockey rink on one side and a pool on the other, and Charlie had spent her whole life on the rink side, until tonight. She stood at the shallow end in her suit, watching the older kids race. Every swimmer in the freestyle final was doing the same stroke, arms windmilling, faces turning sideways to breathe. She nudged her classmate Cole, who was waiting for his heat. "Why does everyone swim exactly the same way in freestyle? Isn't freestyle supposed to mean you can pick anything?"

Cole shrugged, but Jase, towelling off from an earlier race, overheard them. "Freestyle means you can pick any stroke," he said, "but almost every swimmer chooses front crawl, because it's the fastest of the competitive strokes." Charlie stared at the churning lanes. So the rule wasn't that they had to match. They had all figured out the same answer. That meant the stroke itself must have something in it worth copying, and she wanted to know what.

Her own problem was breathing. On Saturday she had tried twenty-five metres of front crawl and ended up coughing, half a length in, while Mr. Ba, the lifeguard, watched from his chair. Afterward she'd sat in the bleachers above the rink, where the Zamboni ground around the ice, and thought about it. Her swim had fallen apart the moment her breathing did. Maybe the two things were connected, and if she could regulate her breathing, turning her head on a steady rhythm instead of whenever she panicked, her arms and legs would keep their economy of motion instead of wasting it. Twenty-five metres of sloppy flailing might be equivalent to ten good ones, she figured, and ten wasn't enough.

In the water now, Charlie pushed off and counted. Breathe every three strokes, no matter what. One, two, breathe. One, two, breathe. The wall came sooner than she expected, and she grabbed it, gasping but whole. Jase leaned over the lane rope. "You made it." Charlie wiped her eyes and said, "Same stroke as you guys. Fastest one, right?"

activity: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
knowledge_domain: to explain why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming
fact: Archaeologists found a workers' town and workers' tombs beside the Giza pyramids, evidence that the builders were organized, fed and honoured laborers rather than slaves.
story:
Eleanor had one job in Ms. Teo's class: explain, out loud, why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids and how the Nile shaped their farming. She also had one problem, and his name was Cruz. "Slaves built them," he whispered during the practice round, drumming his pencil like a chariot race. "I saw it in a movie. Thousands of guys dragging stones with whips cracking behind them." Eleanor's ears went hot. Her notes contradicted him, but her notes were a mess of cookie crumbs and arrows, and Paisley kept giggling at Cruz's whip noises, which did not help.

Ms. Teo, refusing to be their answer machine, sent them to the museum room instead. "A mentor points at the door," she said. "She doesn't carry you through it." The museum room smelled like dust and old glue, and the radiator clanked in the corner like something trying to escape. There, behind smudgy glass, stood a display about the Giza pyramids. Eleanor leaned in. Beside the pyramids, the map showed two things she had not expected: a workers' town, and workers' tombs, sitting right next to the great stone triangles, perpendicular to the model's neat little base, like neighbors waving over a fence.

"They got their own town?" Cruz squinted at the label. "And tombs? Right beside the pyramids?" Eleanor read aloud, wiggling with the joy of it: the workers were organized, fed, and honoured laborers. "Honoured. Like, with respect. You don't build a tomb for someone you're whipping." Cruz's shoulders slumped, then popped back up. "So the movie lied to me." "The movie lied to you," Paisley said solemnly, patting his shoulder. "Let it go."

Back in class, Eleanor stood up and told the whole thing: the Nile flooding every year, laying down black mud for wheat, farmers free in flood season to build. She pointed at the model pyramid, then at the tiny town beside it, then at Cruz. "And they were paid workers, not slaves," she said. Cruz raised his hand and added, "With a town and tombs. I checked." Ms. Teo wrote one word on her clipboard, and Paisley swore it said "bravo."

knowledge_domain: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
fact: A hook is the opening line that grabs attention, such as a question, a surprising fact or a very short story.
story:
The community theatre smelled like dust and old popcorn, and Camille stood on its wobbly stage holding three note cards that trembled in her hand. In two weeks she had to give a two-minute speech at the school assembly, with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and Ms. Müller, who ran the Saturday speaking club at the theatre, had told them the stage was theirs to practice on. The rows of empty red seats stared back at her. "Go ahead," Ms. Müller said from the back row. "Pretend we're a full house."

Camille began the way she always began. "Today I will talk about why our town needs a bike trail." In the seats, Vayda yawned, Aviraj examined his shoelace, and even Ms. Müller's eyes drifted toward the exit sign. Camille stopped, cheeks hot. "That bad, huh?" "Worse," said Vayda cheerfully. "I was thinking about pizza."

Aviraj climbed up next, because he wanted the announcer job at the theatre's spring show and figured a speech club would help. He mimicked Camille's dull opening voice so exactly, flat and droopy, that Vayda laughed so hard she slid off her seat. "Okay, okay," Camille said, but a thought had started ticking. It wasn't the topic that was boring. It was the first line. Something about that first line decided whether people listened at all.

She tried an experiment. Same speech, different opening. "Did you know a turtle in our creek has to cross four roads to lay her eggs?" Heads came up. Vayda leaned forward. Aviraj put down his shoelace. Camille pushed on with her three points and a closing that circled back to the turtle, and when she finished, the seats didn't feel like a staring crowd anymore. "That's a hook," Ms. Müller called out. "A question, a surprising fact, or a very short story, right at the top." Camille wrote the words on the back of her first card in block letters.

They spent the next hour inventing hooks for each other, and Aviraj's were so strange, "Imagine your grandmother is a secret astronaut," that Vayda declared his speech about recycling was now the funniest thing she'd ever heard, even though his town's old recycling bins were so impoverished that half of them had lost their lids. He beamed, because funny was exactly what an announcer needed to be.

On assembly day, Camille walked to the microphone, saw four hundred faces, and asked, "Did you know a turtle in our creek has to cross four roads to lay her eggs?" The gym went quiet, and she smiled. Somewhere in the third row, a hand shot up. "Which turtle?" a boy called out, and Camille said, "Wait for point two."
